sentences.text: Itasuchus featured an elongated, flattened snout with interlocking teeth similar to those of modern crocodilians. The nostrils opened forward and upward near the tip of the snout, while the skull measured approximately 37 cm in length. The lower jaw could reach up to 43 cm, containing 18 teeth, though two are missing from the holotype specimen. Each premaxilla likely held five teeth, with the third being the largest.
Among related species, Itasuchus was likely the heaviest due to its thicker armor.

The genus Itasuchus was first described by Price in 1955. Llewellyn Ivor Price named the animal based on fossils found near Peirópolis. The type species Itasuchus jesuinoi was described from fossils in the Maastrichtian-aged Marília Formation in Uberaba, Brazil. The genus was established by Price in 1955.
The laterally flattened tail and shifted keels of Itasuchus effectively created a paddle.

The family Itasuchidae was established in 2004 to include Itasuchus and Malawisuchus. Carvalho and colleagues coined the family Itasuchidae to unite Itasuchus with Malawisuchus in 2004. The clade name Itasuchidae was revived in 2018 by Pinheiro and colleagues. The Paleobi Database lists Itasuchus as belonging to the parent group Itasuchidae.

Itasuchus lived in river systems during the late Campanian and early Maastrichtian stages. The environment where Itasuchus lived likely had an arid to semi-arid climate that experienced wetter periods. Itasuchus lived from the Campanian to the Maastrichtian, between 83.6 and 66 million years ago.

It is debated whether Caririsuchus camposi should be classified as a species of Itasuchus, a proposal made by Buffetaut that was not widely accepted. The placement of Itasuchus in Trematochampsidae is debated due to potential issues with the holotype of Trematochampsa. The family classification of Itasuchus is debated, with Trematochampsidae being a proposed but uncertain family.
